source_caption:
Brian De Palma and screenwriter Oliver Stone violently subvert the traditional, idealistic immigrant narrative, morphing the classic pursuit of the American Dream into a blood-soaked, terrifying cautionary tale of absolute capitalist excess. The film’s legendarily chaotic, apocalyptic climax—anchored by Tony Montana’s monstrous mountain of cocaine and his iconic, roaring last stand—is far more than just a display of mindless cinematic violence. Al Pacino’s relentlessly unhinged, feral performance masterfully transforms a ruthless, drug-addled kingpin into a modern, tragic Shakespearean monster, brilliantly proving that a relentless, unchecked obsession with power ultimately destroys the very soul it promised to elevate.
⠀
Scarface (1983), directed by Brian De Palma, starring Al Pacino, Michelle Pfeiffer, Steven Bauer. A fiercely ambitious, ruthlessly violent Cuban refugee arrives in 1980s Miami with absolutely nothing, brutally clawing his way to the top of a massive, sun-drenched cocaine empire before his own mounting paranoia and insatiable greed threaten to violently tear it all apart.

source_details.title: Scarface
source_details.synopsis: Scarface is a 1983 American epic crime drama film directed by Brian De Palma from a screenplay by Oliver Stone. It is loosely based on the 1930 novel by Armitage Trail and is a remake of the 1932 film of the same name directed by Howard Hawks. The film stars an ensemble cast led by Al Pacino, who stars as Cuban refugee Tony Montana. In the film, Montana arrives in Miami during the Mariel boatlift and becomes a powerful drug lord. Pacino worked with producer Martin Bregman to develop the project. Bregman and Sidney Lumet both conceived the idea of setting the story during the boatlift.
